contents:
What the event actually was This was not two teams of robots fighting over a ball. Each team fields two attacking robots (yellow, #3 and #5); the goalkeeper is supplied by the organisers (blue, #4, position unknown and able to move). The referee places the ball on five fixed spots in turn, and each spot gets its own attacking play: (1) back zone, (2) midfield point, (3) front zone, (4) corner zone, (5) penalty point. The exact locations of the back, front and corner zones are not published before the event.
Two constraints, both hard:
each spot must be completed within 15 seconds — anything longer is counted as 15 s; except for the penalty, at least one pass must be completed before shooting, or it counts as a direct shot and a foul. Scoring: a goal is +20, no goal 0, ball out 0; each foul is −5 and voids the goal (fouls are shooting directly, entering the penalty area, and touching the ball twice); skipping a spot is −10. The final mark is 80% on-field execution plus 20% technical report.
In other words, the rulebook is a fixed acceptance test: fifteen seconds, one compulsory pass, a keeper that moves. It turns “robot football” from an open problem into a flow problem with two actors, three fouls and five starting points — which is exactly why it can be solved with a script.
The five fixed spots, from the official competition guide: 1 back zone, 2 midfield point, 3 front zone, 4 corner zone, 5 penalty point. Back, front and corner locations are not announced beforehand. The platform gives you exactly two layers The mandated software was SOM 3.4.2, running on the organisers’ machine; teams submitted two kinds of artefact:
A Lua tactics layer — under Team/lua_scripts/play/Package/<scenario>/, one state machine per spot, choreographing who runs where, who receives, when to pass, when to shoot; A C++ skill layer — the built-in passing function was not reliable enough on the real carpet, so we wrote our own skill DLLs into Team/user_skills/ and called them straight from Lua, controlling kick power, kick angle, the facing after receiving the ball, and the shooting direction. Roles are fixed: #1 Goalie, #3 Kicker, #5 Receiver. Writing task.KickerTask("shemen") in Lua ultimately loads user_skills/shemen.dll — the names map one to one, and Lua only passes coordinates, heading and power (kp=127, cp=6 by default).
One spot is three states All five spots share the same skeleton: get the ball → pass → shoot (GetBall → PassBall → Shoot). Below is the back-zone free kick script in full; it is essentially identical to the front-zone and corner versions:
gPlayTable.CreatePlay{ firstState = "GetBall", ["GetBall"] = { switch = function() if Cbuf_cnt((CBall2RoleDist("Receiver") < 30 and CRole2TargetDist("Kicker")< 5),120) then return "PassBall" end end, Kicker=task.GotoPos("Kicker",80,5,KickerRole2BallDir), Receiver = task.GetBall("Receiver","Kicker"), }, ["PassBall"] = { switch = function() if CIsBallKick("Receiver") or CBall2RoleDist("Receiver") < 5 or Cbuf_cnt(ture,120) then return "Shoot" end end, Kicker=task.RobotHalt("Kicker"), Receiver = task.ReceiverTask("chuanqiu"), Goalie = task.Goalie() }, ["Shoot"] = { switch = function() if CIsBallKick("Kicker") then return "finish" end end, Receiver = task.GotoPos("Receiver",-176,-178,0), Kicker = task.KickerTask("shemen"), Goalie = task.Goalie() }, name = "P_Back" } Three details are worth pointing out:
Cbuf_cnt(condition, 120) does not mean “if the condition holds” but “if it has held for 120 consecutive frames”. A single flickering frame resets the counter, so one bad vision reading cannot push the play forward; CBall2RoleDist("Receiver") < 30 checks whether the ball is with #5, and CRole2TargetDist("Kicker") < 5 checks whether #3 has reached its spot. Both must hold before the state advances; during the shot, #5 retreats to (-176, -178) to clear the shooting line — that is not tactics, just basic manners about not standing in front of your own striker. The flowchart from the 2022 technical report (original in Chinese): execute → R to the ball → K to the receiving position → R collects → pass → K collects → R clears the front zone → shoot → end. R is the midfield robot (#5), K the striker (#3). Four things the real field forced on us The three-stage play ran beautifully in simulation. The first on-site session (28 June) dismantled it. The next two months were mostly spent patching four things:
Frame confirmation plus a timeout guard. On the real carpet the robots routinely stopped “just short” of the target, so the transition condition never became true and the play waited forever. From 3 July every stage carries a Cbuf_cnt timer: even if the condition is not met, the timeout forces the next block of instructions, so at least the ball gets kicked.
A guard stage between pass and receive. A missed pass was the most frequent failure: #5 assumed the ball had left, when in fact it was still sitting there. So we inserted a stage between PassBall and Shoot that only advances once the receiver really has the ball, while the receiver keeps running to its spot; the guard duration is tunable through the delay function.
Mirroring the runs left and right. We started with hard-coded “striker stands here, receiver stands there”, and the two robots kept crowding the same point. The later K_* rewrite decides the receiving point from the sign of CGetBallY(): mirrored to -35 / -148 when the ball is in the left half, +35 / +148 in the right half.
Kick power in distance bands. A single fixed power either overshot short passes or undershot long ones, so the power became a piecewise function of the target distance (kp and cp control the flat and chip kicks separately). I made that change on 27 June.
One more item is not technical, but it saved the competition: we prepared two complete script sets. Our own DLLs behaved well in simulation and often barely at all on the field, so we also wrote a second set using only official functions and swapped the whole set on site whenever the custom DLLs failed. That guaranteed we would never score zero.
Results 18 September 2022, field 2, match 1. Two script runs, best result counted:
Run Spots scored Points Total time Fouls First 4 / 5 80 35.68 s 0 Second 2 / 5 40 34.21 s 0 Eighty points and zero fouls in the first run earned a first prize at the provincial final; the national final in October brought a third prize. In July and August we also entered the China Robot and AI Competition circuit — first prize in the Shanghai region, second prize in the national final — although from that line only the two certificates survive, no code and no report.
The number I remember best is 13.94 s: the back-zone free kick, from the referee placing the ball to the ball crossing the line, took almost fourteen seconds — one second under the limit. The technical report is honest about the rest too: simulated scoring went from 50% to 90%, hardware-in-the-loop from 40% to 80%, and per-skill simulation success was 95% for passing, 95% for shooting, 60% for receiving and 100% for penalties. Nearly usable in simulation, barely enough on the field.
Three problems I only saw afterwards Reading through the submitted code while archiving it turned up more problems than expected. All are left untouched — patching them would make the repository disagree with what was actually submitted — and are flagged in 代码导读.md:
Cbuf_cnt(ture, 120) — ture is a typo for true, which in Lua is nil. The timeout guard therefore never fires, and once a pass is missed the P_ series simply sits in PassBall until the fifteen seconds run out. That bug maps exactly onto the “missed pass” difficulty listed in the technical report. The back, front and corner scripts are identical apart from name, with the Kicker standing at (80, 5) in all three. Only the midfield script moved to (130, 5). So the corner spot was actually running the back-zone choreography. Coordinates, thresholds, kp=127, cp=6 are hard-coded across a dozen scripts. Changing one number meant opening seven or eight files, which is why on-site tuning ended up as handwritten notes in test.txt. Looking back, all three have the same root cause: because we had no field, we put parameters inside the code instead of a configuration file. With a parameter table, none of the three would have required a code change.
Material The competition documents, both technical reports, the scanned official score sheet, the four certificates, and the Lua scripts and skill DLLs we wrote are collected in the repository:
https://github.com/yicongl1/iLoboke-Robot-Soccer-2022
It does not include the SOM 3.4.2 platform itself (commercial software of the technical support company), so a clone can be read but not run. The encrypted submission packages — encrypted as the rules required, password since lost — are kept as Release attachments as evidence of what was actually submitted.
summary: Two attacking robots and a goalkeeper that moves, five fixed spots, fifteen seconds each, and at least one pass before any shot. We wrote the tactics as Lua state machines and our own C++ skill DLLs, scoring 80 points without a single foul in the national qualifier.
title: Football robots

contents:
Background MachiKoro is a light, dice-driven strategy board game. The rules are not complicated, but there are many card types and their effects trigger at different moments — a good exercise in object-oriented modelling.
This was a team course project for Algorithms and Programming at Shanghai University in autumn 2022. We built a single-machine Windows console version in C++14, supporting 1-N human players and AI in mixed games.
Résumé summary Stack: C++14, STL, OOP, UML, Visual Studio 2022, Git
Contributed to the MachiKoro core: 15 buildings, 4 landmarks, five-colour settlement, market purchases and win conditions, for 1-N human and AI players. Designed a Card base class with five colour subclasses and polymorphic settlement through the pure virtual action(); used Singleton, a simple factory and Iterator to reduce coupling. Refactored purchasing and settlement, fixing 10+ logic and boundary issues (yellow-card return values, out-of-range market slots, purple-card triggers, Shopping Mall bonus); implemented defensive input parsing and autonomous AI decisions. What we built 15 buildings + 4 landmarks, with complete settlement rules across five card colours Card hierarchy: an abstract Card base class and five subclasses, with action() as a pure virtual function Turn flow: roll dice -> red -> blue/green -> purple -> build one building Two market modes: origin uses all 15 buildings; dlc randomly draws 10 AI play: the AI can roll, choose the number of dice, re-roll and buy on its own Defensive input: regex parsing, single-line input, bounds/funds/duplicate checks My contribution As a team member I worked on core development and debugging, mainly:
the card hierarchy and polymorphic settlement the purchase flow and boundary checks the AI action candidate set input parsing and documentation Outcome The project compiles and runs as a complete game, with mixed human/AI play. Besides the source code, the repository keeps the UML class diagram, course notes, demo videos and the legacy prototype, documenting how it evolved from coursework into a maintainable project.
Source and full documentation: https://github.com/yicongl1/Machikoro
summary: A dice-driven board game in C++14 for 1-N players and AI: 15 buildings, 4 landmarks, five-colour card settlement, market purchases and win conditions.
title: MachiKoro board game in C++

contents:
Context This was my TN10 final internship at ART X BAT, working in MOEX / OPC — execution-phase client representation, scheduling, coordination and site supervision.
I followed three very different operations: a new build, an urban renovation, and the refurbishment of office floors in a high-rise (IGH) building at Paris La Défense (floors 34–39, Tours A/B). The high-rise became the main case study.
The site constraints were concrete:
strict access, visitor and authorisation control; limited delivery dock, delivery slots and storage; heavy trade co-activity and many interfaces; highly repetitive office layouts with regular ceiling grids and technical equipment; a tight schedule and a surge of punch-list items during OPR (pre-handover operations). In this context, MOEX/OPC is not about “recording progress”: it is about turning site information into actionable work — locate, describe, assign, follow up, verify.
What I did Site tracking Attended meetings, took notes and clarified technical points; checked headcount by trade against the planned progress; carried out site inspections, photos and measurements; tracked badges, access rights and technical-area authorisation; coordinated the delivery dock, transport slots, storage, waste and site traffic; updated progress tables by floor and zone; wrote clarification, reminder and traceability emails. Quality and punch list Identified and consolidated punch-list items by trade; structured them in IDCapture: location, package, contractor, description, deadline, photo; maintained statuses: open, contractor-closed, MOE-validated, disputed, rejected; used filters and statistics to prepare follow-up lists; joined OPR inspections and published consolidated lists; set up a dispute form to create a traceable client/contractor process. Tool rollout mapped participants and subcontractors into an account list; checked users, roles and permissions; prepared cleaned, zone-split PDF drawings; designed a three-level contractor / MOE / client validation workflow; configured the “site tracking / OPR / handover” sessions; coordinated with the software vendor; introduced the tool to contractors, shared tutorials and organised training. The problem: a punch-list item without a location fails A useful item answers five questions:
Where: floor, zone, drawing, reference point; What: a sufficiently technical description; Who: the responsible package and contractor; When: deadline or target date; Evidence: photos, status history, acceptance record. During OPR the number of items rises quickly. In repetitive office spaces, the same defect can appear dozens of times. To reduce input, teams often create a “general item” (réserve générale) grouping several occurrences into one record.
On paper this is efficient. On site, the record loses its precise location: a contractor may fix some occurrences and miss others, while the MOE cannot check how many points existed or whether all of them are closed.
The result: input becomes easier, but verification, reminders and communication become harder; the risk of omissions, duplicates and untreated items rises.
OpenCV prototype The goal was not to replace people, but to test whether a site photo can produce usable location information. I built two pipelines.
Case A — missing sprinkler rosette The test image contains a manual red circle:
convert BGR to HSV; isolate the two red hue ranges around 0° and 180°; merge the masks; apply closing and opening; extract external contours and filter small areas; convert the main contour into a bounding box. Case A: the red annotation becomes a candidate bounding box. This validates segmentation → contour → location; it does not detect the defect itself. The chain is stable when the visual signal is strong, but it detects the annotation, not the missing rosette.
Case B — open ceiling plenum This case is closer to reality and does not rely on annotation:
grayscale and Gaussian blur; blackhat with a wide rectangular kernel to enhance dark joints; Canny edges; HoughLinesP for horizontal and vertical segments; merge nearby positions and rebuild the ceiling grid; split into cells and compute mean, standard deviation and Laplacian texture energy; select “abnormal” cells; inside those cells, use blackhat, Otsu thresholding, morphology and area/aspect-ratio/local-contrast filters to find elongated dark openings. Case B: candidate openings on the ceiling grid. Results are fragmented; shadows, ducts and lighting changes create false positives. The pipeline produces candidate regions, but one opening may produce several boxes. Site visuals vary too much for fixed rules; a punch-list item is a contractual and engineering concept, not just a dark area.
Results and limits Assisted localisation is useful: a photo can become a mask, contour, candidate box or grid cell — the first step towards pre-filling an item. A single detection is not enough: a representative annotated dataset, a defect taxonomy by package, an independent validation set and acceptance metrics are required. The reasonable automation is assistance: propose a zone, pre-fill a record, then let the MOE confirm. Supervised learning was not trained during the internship because of time and missing annotations; the report frames it as a perspective, not a delivered result. Public poster: problem, method, experiment and limits. Original deliverables have been redacted. Links Company showcase: https://www.artxbat.fr/realisations/bureaux-coeur-defense-pour-bnp-real-estate/ Public code and redacted material: https://github.com/yicongl1/TN10-MOEX-OPC-Portfolio Academic record: /en/undergraduate/utc/#course-TN10
summary: Supported MOEX/OPC on the Cœur Défense office refurbishment (floors 34–39): site inspections, access and logistics coordination, punch-list tracking in IDCapture, and OpenCV experiments for locating ceiling openings and missing sprinkler rosettes.
title: Punch-list tracking and assisted localisation on site

contents:
What kind of podcast is it “The Podcast of Engineers” was started by engineering students and enthusiasts from UTSEUS (Université de Technologie Sino-Européenne de Shanghai, Shanghai University), with five coordinators splitting the work of topic selection, guest outreach, recording and publishing. The show interviews engineers, former engineers, founders, managers and professors in Chinese, French and English — not about the “responsibilities” in a job description, but about what concrete people actually run into in concrete work.
We believe in one sentence: engineering without humanity is devoid of soul. So conversations often start from robotics, aerospace, civil engineering or computer science and wander into literature, philosophy, history, language, art, ecology and psychology.
My role As one of the five coordinators I worked on topic planning, guest outreach and the production flow, and hosted some of the episodes. Cross-language production is also something I care about: the same show has to stay listenable and information-dense in three linguistic contexts.
Production flow Topics: find the intersection between the guest’s work and what listeners actually wonder about Outline: agree with the guest on the boundaries of the conversation beforehand, avoiding vague “success story” questions Recording: mostly remote, 60–90 minutes per episode Publishing: Bilibili as the main platform, mirrored on the website (Hugo + GitHub Pages), episode metadata managed in Markdown Visuals: a consistent cover system across all 14 episodes Episode 001 Guests The 14 guests span two engineering education systems and two career paths: data and engineering roles at Meituan, Microsoft, Google, McDonald’s and Equativ on one side; professors and a former president from École Centrale de Lyon, Paris-Saclay, Kaiserslautern-Landau and CUHK on the other — plus an SDN pioneer and an AI founder.
The full episode list is below, or go straight to the Bilibili collection.
summary: A trilingual engineer interview podcast run with friends from UTSEUS — 14 episodes and 14 guests from academia and industry, from Meituan, Microsoft and Google to the former president of École Centrale de Lyon.
title: The Podcast of Engineers

contents:
Context This was my TN09 final internship at UTC’s Avenues laboratory (EA 7284), contributing to BEST — a project building the theoretical foundation for “territorial system balance” and preparing a multi-scale decision-support tool for planners and policymakers.
Growing territories face four tensions: saturated transport, territorial inequality, rapid urbanisation and high housing costs. Existing models (urban dynamics, MCDA, PSR/DPSIR) treat housing, mobility, environment and economy separately; none offers a unified representation of the territorial system.
BEST aims to:
build a theoretical framework for “balance” applied to territorial systems; characterise a dynamic, multi-scale territorial balance whose final criterion is residents’ well-being; prepare the conceptual model, indicators and data for a future decision-support tool. What I did Three independent systematic reviews, an operationalisation of concepts into indicators, and a quantitative exploration of their relationships.
1. PRISMA systematic reviews Searched Scopus, Google Scholar, HAL and PROSPERO, mainly in French and English, prioritising the last ten years, and managed references with Zotero.
The protocol followed PRISMA: identify studies → remove duplicates → screen titles and abstracts → full-text reading and inclusion criteria. Each article was classified as relevant / partially relevant / not relevant, with a justification.
Theme Articles analysed Guiding question Territorial system 360 How is a territory organised, and at which scales? Well-being 120 Which dimensions make up residents’ well-being? Territorial balance 80 Which levers support harmonious development? Total 560 2. Indicator frameworks Territorial system: the 134 urban sustainability indicators of Agenda 21, classified by economic, social, environmental and institutional dimensions, supplemented with French sources (INSEE, ADEME, eaufrance, ATMO France, ministries). Well-being: the 11 dimensions of the OECD Better Life Index — housing, income, jobs, community, education, environment, civic engagement, health, life satisfaction, safety, work-life balance — distinguishing objective (homicide rate) and subjective (feeling safe walking alone at night) indicators. Each row documents the definition, official source and calculation method, so the indicators can be implemented directly.
3. Correlation analysis The goal was to check the internal consistency of the indicator set and identify dependencies to include in the model.
OECD CSV (long format) → pivot country × indicator → Pearson matrix → seaborn heatmaps → comparison by country group Correlation heatmap of 22 OECD Better Life Index indicators. Most relationships match common sense; a few anomalies are kept as questions for later modelling. Representative relationships:
Relationship r Reading Life expectancy ↔ dwellings without basic facilities −0.85 Poor sanitation undermines health Personal earnings ↔ life satisfaction +0.80 Perceived well-being is strongly linked to financial stability Unemployment rate ↔ student skills −0.68 Qualification and employability are linked One anomaly was kept: water quality correlates strongly with employment and life satisfaction. It is more likely a sample-structure effect than a causal mechanism, and needs explanation in later modelling.
4. Conceptual modelling Combined Forrester’s urban dynamics (population / housing / economic activity and feedback loops), MCDA, PSR / DPSIR and a sensitivity model into a multi-scale framework.
Tools: Vensim (system dynamics), ArcGIS (spatial analysis and mapping), Python (indicator processing), Excel (indicator tables).
Results A structured corpus of 560 articles and three conceptual reviews defining territorial systems, well-being and balance, and their links. Two ready-to-use indicator frameworks with official sources and formulas, providing the quantitative base for the future tool. A reproducible correlation analysis (code, data, figures) showing that most Better Life Index relationships match expectations, while isolating anomalies. A contribution to the BEST conceptual framework and decision-support algorithm. TN09 academic poster: problem, territorial system, well-being, balance and the multi-scale framework. Limits The corpus is mainly English; French literature was used complementarily, not systematically. Correlation is not causation: the analysis is exploratory, without significance testing or control for confounders. Missing values were filled with 0 following the original analysis, which may bias some correlations for incomplete countries. Indicator units, scales and periods remain heterogeneous; aggregating them into a single index was not the task of this internship. Links Research code and public material: https://github.com/yicongl1/TN09-BEST-Territorial-Well-Being Academic record: /en/undergraduate/utc/#course-TN09
summary: Contributed to the BEST project at UTC’s Avenues laboratory: three PRISMA systematic reviews (560 articles), two indicator frameworks for territorial systems and well-being, an OECD correlation analysis, and a multi-scale conceptual framework supported by Vensim and ArcGIS.
title: BEST: multi-scale territorial balance and urban well-being

contents:
Background A photovoltaic module’s I-V curve has a single maximum-power point (MPP), and its position moves continuously with irradiance and temperature. If the load pins the operating point, the module can drift far from the MPP and lose 20-30% of its production. The job of MPPT is to keep the operating point on the MPP with a DC-DC converter.
This was the BA04 “Renewable Energy Conversion and Management” course project at UTC, a team of four, defended in June 2024. The object was a Kyocera KC200GT (200 Wp polycrystalline module). We built the PV module, a SEPIC converter and the controller in Simulink, then drove the model with one full year of measurements from UTC’s STELLA platform. The report compares four algorithms: P&O, incremental conductance (INC), an improved P&O (P&OA) and fuzzy logic.
Data and simulation Data: 1 April 2023 to 31 March 2024, 366 days; one sample per minute, 1440 points per day; irradiance, ambient temperature and cell temperature. Model: the module is described by a parameterised exponential model; the solver step is 2 s, and daily runs are concatenated into a full year. Analysis: instantaneous power is integrated into daily energy (kWh) and divided by the incident solar energy of the same day (kWh/m²): E_day = Σ P(t) · Δt / 3.6e6 [kWh] η = Σ E_day(PV) / Σ E_day(G) The code has three layers: loadYearData / loadDayData read the Excel files and rebuild the time axis, runSimulation / runYearSimulation run the model, and runAnalysis computes energy, efficiency, CSV files and the comparison figure. Every path is relative to the repository root, so the project can be moved freely.
My contribution In the four-person split I owned P&O and its improved version P&OA:
implementing both duty-cycle perturbation schemes in Simulink injecting the per-minute irradiance and temperature series into the From Workspace blocks, one day at a time batching all 366 days and concatenating the instantaneous power into a yearly series computing daily and annual energy, efficiency, and the comparison plots rewriting and tidying the code after the course: function split, relative paths, README and reproduction steps The other group methods (incremental conductance, fuzzy logic) are kept in archive/other_methods/; the report and defence material are in docs/.
Results Annual energy: 180.28 kWh with P&O, 179.36 kWh with P&OA — a difference of about 0.5%. Over a full year the two power curves almost overlap. P&OA’s advantage shows up mainly during irradiance transients and in steady-state oscillation when the step is badly tuned. The gain sweep in the report (0.1 / 0.5 / 1) shows the first two settings behaving similarly, while a gain of 1 noticeably lowers the recovered power — too large a step amplifies the oscillation. An honest conclusion: with one-minute data over a whole year, “annual energy” smooths away the transient differences between the algorithms. A fairer comparison of P&O and P&OA uses settling time after a step, steady-state power ripple, and tracking efficiency at different step sizes.
Source, Simulink models, raw data and report: https://github.com/yicongl1/MPPT-direct
summary: Modelled a Kyocera KC200GT module in MATLAB/Simulink and compared P&O against the improved P&OA over 366 days of per-minute irradiance and temperature measured by UTC’s STELLA platform, in terms of annual energy and efficiency.
title: Photovoltaic MPPT — P&O and its improved variant

contents:
What the event actually was The arena is 4 × 4 m, with the launch pad and three drop zones A, B and C in the corners. Zone A is a 500 mm target ring, scored by how far the payload lands from the centre; B and C carry different patterns that have to be recognised before releasing. A building stands between the start and zone A, and there are lamp posts on the B–C line — obstacles and pattern order are drawn on site, and the posts can shift by ±500 mm, precisely to defeat open-loop scripts that just follow a timer.
The payload is a cone with a spherical cap: 60 mm cap diameter, 50 mm base, 65 mm tall (70 mm limit). Compared with a cylinder it sits lower, tips less on landing and is less sensitive to rotor wash.
The flow is simple: load and secure → a single start command begins the clock → drop at A, B and C in order, one attempt each → B and C require crossing obstacles → after C, return and land to stop the clock.
Scoring details that shape the strategy: +5 per obstacle correctly crossed; +3 for returning inside the time limit; the payload must land upright or it does not count; a coefficient rewards autonomy; each team flies two rounds of five minutes, weighted 50% each with the best kept; a 20-second stop ends the round, and touching the safety net or an obstacle ends the run outright.
Arena and zones from the task statement: a 4000 × 4000 field, zone A as a 500 mm target ring, zones B and C identified by pattern, and a 600 × 600 launch pad at the bottom. One stack in the air, one on the ground The aircraft carries a PX4 flight controller and a Jetson Nano. The Nano does three jobs: MAVROS for talking to the flight controller, the RealSense T265 VIO pipeline (through vision_to_mavros into the EKF), and the downward CSI camera for pattern recognition. The ground station is a second Ubuntu machine running the mission program. The two talk over ROS networking, which means ROS_MASTER_URI, ROS_IP and /etc/hosts all have to agree before take-off — and when they do not, the symptom is “the aircraft flies but ignores commands”, which is why Chapter 1 of our operating manual is entirely about networking.
That is also how the work was split: flight control and mission flow, vision, and structure/release mechanism, four lines meeting in the same launch file.
Indoor test session: the mission node and status printouts on the ground station, the aircraft doing altitude and hover checks in an empty hall. One state machine, five actions com_node is the mission program. Given a list of waypoints, it repeats the same block for each one:
for (int i = 0; i < num_fly + 1; i++) { fly_high(i, desire_z); // from 0.3 m, step up to cruise altitude fly_to(i); // approach the waypoint, arrived when all three axes are within 0.15 m landing(); // step down, landed when |vz| < 0.1 m/s and altitude < 0.1 m unload(i + 1); // below 0.2 m: hold 3 s, send /servo, hold 2 s more } Four calls, but every one of them hides the same rule: setpoints have to be walked over, never jumped.
void add_target(int i) { for (int j = 0; j < 3; j++) { if (abs(next_point[j] - fly_point[i + 1][j]) > 0.3) { if (next_point[j] > fly_point[i + 1][j]) { next_point[j] -= change; } else { next_point[j] += change; } } else { next_point[j] = fly_point[i + 1][j]; } } } With change between 0.02 and 0.05 m and the loop running at 20 Hz, the aircraft sees a smooth trajectory instead of a step input. Publishing the destination directly makes the controller fight the frame to catch up. This is the least glamorous line in the project and the one that decides whether the aircraft looks calm on video.
Three things only the field teaches You have five seconds after arming to enter OFFBOARD. If PX4 does not receive external setpoints shortly after arming, it re-arms itself and the aircraft never leaves the ground. The on-site sequence was fixed accordingly: switch to OFFBOARD first, then arm — and never use AUTO.TAKEOFF.
send_info_node is a 20 Hz safety net. Whatever the mission is doing, if the aircraft is not yet in OFFBOARD or not armed, this node keeps publishing setpoints. Without it, the instant of switching modes manually is enough for the controller to decide it has no external command and drop out of the mode.
The landing target height is negative. landing() drives the setpoint z down to −0.5 m, below the floor. The aircraft cannot go there, so it keeps pushing down until speed and altitude fall under the thresholds. A hack, but a reliable one.
The release itself is even cruder: wait until altitude is below 0.2 m, hold position for 3 seconds so the airframe and payload settle, send one byte to the Arduino, then hold 2 seconds more so the aircraft does not climb away and drag the payload with it.
The release mechanism The cargo bay is fully enclosed: four acrylic rods and two outer rings, heavily perforated to save weight. Each bay has its own servo whose arm presses the payload against the frame so it stays still in flight; on command the arm rotates, the payload drops vertically, and the bay keeps flying and can be reused.
CAD model of the cargo bay and servo release: one servo arm per bay holds the payload until the drop command arrives. The Nano-to-Arduino link is a single-byte serial protocol: 1 / 2 / 3 open the corresponding bay, 6 resets all of them, anything else is ignored, at 9600 baud. The device is pinned to /dev/arduino through a udev alias, otherwise every replug moves it between ttyACM0 and ttyACM1 — a reconfiguration you only want to do once.
The vision half The downward camera runs at 960 × 540 and the detector is pure contour geometry, not template matching. The test is a single dimensionless ratio, perimeter² over area:
circle: perimeter² ÷ (4 × area) ≈ π, tolerance 0.4; square: perimeter² ÷ area ≈ 16, tolerance 2. Pre-processing is bilateral filtering → Canny(24, 144) → a 9 × 9 closing to bridge broken edges → a 3 × 3 opening to kill highlights, then findContours filtered by the test above. The centroid comes from the contour moments, the pixel offset (480 − x, 270 − y) is converted into metres with a pinhole model, and that offset nudges the drop point.
The advantage is weight: it runs on a Nano and needs no training. The disadvantage is recorded in the known issues below.
Results First prize at the university qualifier (October 2022) and the Grand Prize at the municipal final (December 2022).
What decided the run was not how steadily the aircraft flew but how many of the three drops landed upright. The final version flew blind to the waypoint, applied one visual correction, then landed and settled before releasing — so the residual error came mostly from T265 drift rather than from recognition accuracy.
In the same semester we used the system as the group project of a French-taught project management course: Gantt chart, four decks on risk, resources, scheduling and communication, a survey, a promo video and a full set of weekly plans. Sharing one set of material between the technical and the PM project was the best value decision of that year.
Known issues The archived code is left exactly as it ran; the problems are documented rather than fixed:
the vision test is single-frame with no multi-frame consistency check: one spurious contour that satisfies the test immediately sends its offset to the flight controller; the focal lengths fx = 4.476, fy = 5.96 and the sensor size were calibrated for that one CSI camera — changing the camera requires recalibration; desire_z (cruise altitude) takes five different values across the launch files — 0.5 / 1.0 / 1.4 / 2.0 / 5.0 m — and you must check which one is live before flying; landing_quadrotor.cpp, take_off_test.cpp and fly.cpp are half-finished: they depend on a message type that does not exist, or do not compile. Do not roslaunch them. Material The rules, the task statement, the operating manual, the complete ROS workspace and 14 debugging recordings (seven of them public in the release) are in the repository:
https://github.com/yicongl1/Drone-Delivery-2022
The archive was reorganised into six levels — competition material, technical documents, code, recordings, project management course, miscellany — compressing 630 files and 4.7 GB down to 391 files and 4.5 GB. Git tracks only 312 files (about 295 MB); the recordings live in the release. Teammate names were replaced with neutral placeholders throughout.
summary: Autonomously crossing obstacles, recognising patterns and making three pinpoint drops inside a 4 × 4 m arena. PX4 plus a Jetson Nano, with a ROS state machine driving take-off, cruise, descent and release.
title: Smart delivery drone

contents:
The question Science communication is usually treated as something downstream of research: the results are in, then we figure out how to explain them to the public. This TZ asks about the other side: if science mediation happens upstream, can it be the method itself?
The report is titled “Développement méthodologique par la médiation scientifique” (methodological development through science mediation), supervised by Maxime Hachette and Manuela Sechilariu. It is not a portfolio of outreach pieces but a methodological study: literature, field, proposal.
1. Literature: narrowing the corpus Platform and query: HAL, keyword “médiation scientifique”, no year or language restriction, restricted document types (journal articles, conference papers, reports, etc.) Screening: 183 records identified → 2 near-duplicates removed → 181 screened on metadata → 114 excluded (too peripheral, not analytical enough, or closer to advertising, book reviews and event material) → 67 retained Close reading: the 67 map the field; 11 papers read in depth form the analytical core What the close reading yields is not a catalogue of definitions but four tensions:
Mediation vs. popularisation: popularisation is a top-down simplification and transmission; mediation emphasises dialogue, interaction and feedback — the public is not only a receiver but potentially a contributor to knowledge production Form vs. content: form (style, cover, editorial choices) is not decoration; it takes part in constructing the relation between content and reader Research vs. field: the role of mediation keeps being redistributed between research and local practice Institutional expectations vs. actual appropriation: a gap remains between what institutions expect from mediation and what publics actually do with it 2. Field: a classroom session on electric mobility On 1 April 2026, at Lycée Charles de Gaulle in Compiègne, I assisted — as an assistant observer — a postdoctoral researcher from the AVENUES lab during a science-mediation session on electric mobility.
My position was not that of the main speaker but of an observer placed close to the device: preparing the material, following the session, watching students’ reactions, noting the moments of attention, understanding and hesitation.
Three observations:
The quiz captures attention quickly, giving the session an immediate interactive entry point How questions are phrased decides whether discussion opens up: what matters is not just asking, but wording, accessibility and openness The quality of visual support matters: slide clarity, chart readability and overall visual coherence directly affect attention and understanding This observation pulls mediation from the level of texts back to the level of the device: a mediation session can surface clues about understanding, representations and cognitive obstacles.
3. Proposal: a four-step methodology Table 1 in the report turns the mediation setting into research material:
Device What is observed Data produced Potential use for research Interactive quiz Correct or wrong answers, hesitations, level Indicators of understanding, fuzzy notions, representations Building cognitive and informational variables Participatory workshop Exchanges, arguments, prioritisation of problems Verbatims, perceived obstacles, usage categories Enriching hypotheses, discussing indicators Visual support / slides / infographics Attention, appropriation, ability to reformulate Indicators of readability and clarity Testing the usability of research outputs Discussion with actors Operational constraints, disagreements, validation Experience feedback, institutional needs, context variables Adjusting the operational relevance of tools Hence a four-step framework:
Conceptual clarification: define science mediation and distinguish mediation, popularisation and co-construction Observation and characterisation: observe mediation devices and identify how they actually work Analytical translation: reformulate observed feedback into categories, indicators and qualitative variables Methodological articulation: connect these variables with other methods — qualitative surveys, GIS, modelling What it means Mediation is no longer just “knowledge transfer” at the end of research, but a space where data emerge: it makes visible dimensions that spatial or technical data alone struggle to capture — the legibility of devices, cognitive load, informational obstacles, and the gap between theoretical accessibility and actual appropriation.
The report is explicit about its limits: the review is targeted rather than exhaustive, the close-read sub-corpus is small, and the framework is a proposal, not a protocol already implemented at scale.
Next step This TZ grew directly into a doctoral application: the SOUND project builds science mediation into the research design as a methodological component (32 days per year).
summary: Final-year project “Développement méthodologique par la médiation scientifique” — a PRISMA-style review (183→67 references), one classroom field observation and a four-step methodological framework arguing that science mediation can be the research protocol itself, not just downstream dissemination.
title: TZ: Science communication as method

contents:
The project In European cross-border territories marked by institutional and energy discontinuities, does the electric mobility transition narrow or widen inequalities of access?
Cross-border spaces are not simple “transit zones”: they are made of dense daily commuting flows, cut by different regulations, tariffs, standards and energy systems on either side. Around areas with strong economic and land-price differentials such as Luxembourg, this cut is especially visible — living on one side and working on the other directly amplifies travel constraints and structural vulnerability.
The core concept is access ergonomics (ergonomie d’accès): it accounts not only for distance and time but also for organisational, economic and cognitive constraints. Applied to electric mobility, it means going beyond the “are there enough charging stations” view to look at comprehension costs, technical management costs and range anxiety.
Research question Under what conditions does the electric mobility transition reduce inequalities of access to mobility, and in which situations does it risk reinforcing them — particularly in cross-border territories marked by institutional and energy discontinuities?
Three hypotheses The border is an amplifier: the discontinuities specific to cross-border spaces amplify inequalities in access ergonomics, which result from a combination of spatial, economic, energy and informational factors PV and smart charging have distributive effects: integrating charging infrastructure into smart energy systems (photovoltaics, smart charging) improves environmental performance but produces differentiated distributive effects across territories and user profiles Coordinated policy is the key lever: policies coordinated at the cross-border level are crucial to reducing these inequalities Methods Spatial analysis: GIS and multi-criteria methods comparing theoretical accessibility with actual conditions of use Qualitative surveys: interviews with cross-border workers to understand charging practices, adaptation strategies and perceived constraints Indicators and typology: an access-ergonomics index (spatial, economic, energy, informational dimensions) feeding a typology of cross-border populations Multi-agent modelling: simulating policy scenarios — business as usual, stronger cross-border coordination, smart charging development Four phases Phase Months Content 1 · Scientific framing and data model M1–M9 Literature, problematisation, data-model structure, exploratory interviews, GIS database 2 · Indicators and systematic collection M10–M15 Indicator construction, cross-country data harmonisation, exploratory analysis, access-ergonomics index 3 · Modelling and scenarios M16–M26 Multi-agent modelling, validation workshops, scenario workshops 4 · Writing and transfer M27–M36 Manuscript, articles, digital atlas, cross-border seminar Science mediation: 32 days a year This is not “some outreach on the side” but workload written into the methodology:
Exploratory phase: identify key actors and surface variables absent from databases — the cognitive load of trip planning, informational obstacles, interoperability problems, the gap between theoretical accessibility and actual appropriation Indicator phase: participatory workshops, user tests and intermediate outputs (maps, visualisations) to test the relevance, legibility and appropriability of indicators Validation phase: intermediate validation of modelling results Transfer phase: cross-border seminars, digital atlas and teaching materials Deliverables Doctoral manuscript; at least one mid-term journal article (typology of cross-border populations and access inequalities); follow-up articles (modelling and scenarios); a digital atlas and teaching materials; a cross-border seminar.
Fieldwork A comparative sweep of several French borders first, then a deeper focus on the Franco-German-Swiss border.
Status This page draws on the doctoral project proposal dated 8 April 2026 (candidature SOUND); the audition has been completed. It continues the TZ line of work: mediation is not the epilogue of research but part of its design.
summary: The SOUND doctoral proposal asks whether the electric mobility transition narrows or widens inequalities of access in European cross-border territories marked by institutional and energy discontinuities — three hypotheses, a four-phase 36-month plan, and 32 days a year of science mediation built into the method.
title: PhD proposal SOUND: access ergonomics for electric mobility in cross-border territories

contents:
Background Between 2021 and 2022 I worked my way from C# fundamentals and Unity basics to four playable Unity prototypes and eight C# console exercises. Most of them started as tutorials or classroom exercises, then grew levels, UI, state machines, particles, sound and my own gameplay tweaks.
The point of this repository is not to show polish, but to keep the learning trail: what the problem was, which API solved it, and how it changed later.
The four Unity prototypes Rolling-ball arcade collection (3D / multi-scene): a main menu links three mini-games — rolling-ball levels, a maze and a pull-the-box puzzle — plus a first-person controller demo. Practised the difference between Rigidbody velocity and force, OnTriggerEnter / OnCollisionEnter, SceneManager transitions, Time.timeScale pausing, coroutines and UGUI. Dragon shooter (2D / vertical shooter): movement with fire-rate cooldown, random enemy spawning, hit flash and explosions, a Boss patrol state machine, and an orthographic camera that adapts to the screen ratio. Practised Instantiate / Destroy, 2D triggers, Mathf.Clamp and UV-scrolling backgrounds. Colour runner (3D / endless runner): the character runs forward automatically, Space jumps, J switches between red and green; landing on a platform of the other colour is fatal. Practised Rigidbody.velocity, collision tags, Animator, particle prefabs and a singleton GameMode. Character movement (3D / character controller): a minimal third-person demo — Input.GetAxis builds a world-space direction, transform.LookAt sets the facing, and the character moves by speed * Time.deltaTime. C# fundamentals Eight standalone .NET Framework 4.7.2 console projects covering:
singleton managers, object arrays, a boxing match 1D/2D arrays and in-place List filtering object copying, constructors and named arguments weighted gacha draws and cumulative probability turn-based combat, skill states, damage and healing over time Dictionary operations and safe deletion while iterating classes, state constraints and a small interactive menu Running and downloading Three games are packaged as Windows 64-bit builds in release-assets/ and published on GitHub Releases. Unzip and run the .exe; if SmartScreen appears, choose “More info -> Run anyway”.
For the Unity projects, install 2021.3 LTS through Unity Hub. The C# exercises load together from csharp-exercises/CSharpExercises.sln in Visual Studio.
Notes The projects keep Assets, Packages and ProjectSettings; generated folders such as Library and Temp are not committed. They use the legacy Input Manager (Input.GetAxis), not the new Input System. Some scripts still contain learning-stage comments, debug code and unused fields; the priority is readable, runnable code. Third-party assets (first-person controller, character model, effects and audio) remain under their original licences and are not covered by the repository’s code licence. Source and builds: https://github.com/yicongl1/Unity-Portfolio
summary: Four Unity prototypes (rolling-ball arcade, dragon shooter, colour runner, character movement) and eight C# console exercises, covering Rigidbody physics, collisions and triggers, UGUI, scene management, coroutines, Animator, particles and audio. Three Windows builds are available from GitHub Releases.
title: Unity game development learning portfolio

contents:
Background This was the final project of IA02 “Problem Solving and Logic Programming” at UTC. The course supplied a referee server (gndserver) and an HTTP client (gndclient.py) handling registration, pairing, timing, legality checks and state synchronisation. Our job was the AI core, jeux.py: board modelling, legal-move generation, position evaluation and search.
The opponents are two two-player hex games designed by Mark Steere: Gopher and Dodo. Neither rule set is complicated, but hex adjacency and the counter-intuitive “no legal move means you win” rule make legal-move and terminal detection easier to get wrong than in ordinary board games.
Rules Gopher
The board starts empty; Red plays first and may place anywhere; every later move must touch exactly one enemy piece and zero friendly pieces; no pass is allowed; the last player able to place a piece wins. A hex board of size n has 3n(n-1)+1 cells: 37 for n=4 and 91 for n=6.
Dodo
Pieces are placed at the start according to the server’s corners or one_line layout; each move shifts one of your pieces one cell straight or diagonally forward, onto an empty cell; if you have no legal move on your turn, you win — the opposite of the usual chess convention. Implementation Board: axial coordinates (x, y) represent the hex grid; initialize_board builds the n=4/6 cells and the Dodo starting layout. Legal moves (legals): Gopher scans the neighbours of enemy pieces and keeps empty cells with exactly one enemy and no friendly neighbour; Dodo uses three forward directions per colour, with in-bounds and empty-target checks. Transitions (apply_action): Gopher places a piece; Dodo clears the origin and fills the destination. Evaluation: the current version uses a mobility heuristic, -len(legals(...)) — fewer available moves means a worse score. Search: minmax plus memoize, keyed on the full board, depth, side to maximise, root player, board size and game name. The root enumerates moves and searches four more plies, five half-moves in total. Game shell: prints an ASCII board each turn, dispatches to the Gopher or Dodo strategy from the server’s game name, and leaves the course-provided gndclient.py untouched. Results and limits With gndserver.exe -game gopher -random running locally, test_client.py completes a full game and prints Ending: 1 wins with a score of 1 and Red wins!.
Rough local measurements (Windows 11, Python 3.14):
Dodo 4×4, one move at depth 4: about 4.5 s; Gopher 4×4 against a random opponent, full game: about 1.7 s. The limitations are explicit:
no time management — a fixed depth of 4 can time out on 6×6 boards; the evaluation only counts mobility and ignores terminal states; legals rescans state repeatedly, so the real cost is close to O(n⁴); Gopher always opens at (0,0) instead of searching the first move; the memoisation cache is unbounded and grows across games; there are no automated tests, only manual and scripted checks. Course archive The repository’s tp/ folder also keeps the IA02 exercises and tutorial sheets: propositional and first-order logic, SAT (including a Sudoku encoding and Gophersat samples), Prolog (family relations, Mastermind), ASP with Clingo, and a Minimax tic-tac-toe. They are independent of the Gopher & Dodo project and serve as a complete learning archive.
Source and rule documents: https://github.com/yicongl1/Gopher-and-Dodo
summary: An AI for Mark Steere’s two-player hex games Gopher and Dodo: axial-coordinate board, legal-move generation, a mobility evaluation and memoised Minimax search.
title: Gopher & Dodo hex-board game AI

contents:
Background This was the BA08 “Data Science for the Smart City” course project at UTC, submitted in June 2024. The assignment allowed either a smart-city use case built from scratch (Level 1) or replaying and improving a public case (Level 2). We chose Level 2, using the Kaggle notebook NYC Airbnb: EDA, Visualization, Regression as a baseline, then adding three improvements: a new city and original data source, features mined from the title, and price-segmented modelling.
Data Source: the Inside Airbnb Bordeaux snapshot, data/listings.csv, 11,854 rows × 18 columns, latin-1 encoded; Target: nightly price (€); 8,162 non-missing values, median €82, mean €115, max €5,300; Only the five largest districts are kept (Bordeaux, Mérignac, Talence, Pessac, Bègles): 9,033 listings, about 76%; Samples used for modelling after cleaning: 2,630 low-price (< €100) and 1,629 high-price (> €100) listings, 4,259 in total. host_name is dropped not only because it carries no signal for price, but also for ethical reasons: no inference should be made about real individuals.
Features and cleaning The name column looks like Rental unit in Bordeaux · ★New · 2 bedrooms · 1 bath. Five new columns are extracted with regular expressions:
note: guest rating, with New mapped to −1; number_of_bedrooms / number_of_beds / number_of_baths: Studio counts as one bedroom and Half-bath as 0.5 bath; type_of_baths: private or shared. Cleaning: missing reviews_per_month becomes 0; rows missing price, note or the three capacity features are dropped; prices and counts are heavily right-skewed, so they are log10-transformed, including the target.
The EDA covers histograms and boxplots, Folium maps coloured by district and room type, a correlation heatmap, and a one-way ANOVA with pairwise comparisons testing whether the district significantly affects price (low-price segment, p ≪ 0.05).
Modelling Two preprocessing pipelines, each trained on both price segments with four models:
Model 1 Model 2 Numeric features log10 transform quantile qcut bins (2–3 levels) Categorical features one-hot (drop_first=True) one-hot (drop_first=True) Feature count 88 57 Models linear regression, random forest (max_depth=8, 100 trees), Ridge, Lasso same Tuning GridSearchCV over alpha same Validation KFold (8/10) + 70/30 split same Metrics are computed in log10(price) space: RMSE = 0.09 corresponds to roughly 10^0.09 − 1 ≈ 23% relative error.
Results Random forest with Model 1 wins on both segments: test R² = 0.52 for low price and 0.55 for high price; linear models plateau around 0.4 (0.41 and 0.46), pointing to non-linear relationships and many unobserved drivers (decoration, view, seasonality, events); the binned pipeline (Model 2) is consistently worse for every model — turning continuous variables into categories throws information away; the three capacity features mined from the title are essential: without them, some models fall below R² = 0.1; random forest overfits: R² = 0.68 on the low-price training set versus 0.52 on the test set. Limitations The sample is small (4,259 listings, only 1,629 in the high-price segment), the data is a single snapshot with no seasonality, features such as surface, renovation, view and transport are missing, the regex extraction fails on non-standard titles, and metrics live in log10 space. Natural next steps are SHAP explanations, XGBoost/LightGBM and a wider hyper-parameter search.
Links Source, notebook, report, defence slides and DataCamp certificates: https://github.com/yicongl1/Bordeaux-Airbnb
summary: An end-to-end study of 11,854 Bordeaux listings from Inside Airbnb: EDA, maps and ANOVA, five features mined from the listing title, and a 100 € price split comparing linear regression, random forest, Ridge and Lasso. Random forest reaches a test R² of 0.52 (low price) and 0.55 (high price).
title: Bordeaux Airbnb price prediction

contents:
Background This was the UR06 “Geomatics” course project at UTC (A23), done in a team of two. The brief required using only raw geographic layers (BD TOPO, ADMIN EXPRESS, Enedis, CORINE) — no pre-built heat-island or LCZ layers — and building the whole vector-to-raster chain in ArcGIS, ending with a heatwave sensitivity map of Dunkirk and a report of about 20 pages.
The original report is lost. The documents in the repository were reconstructed from the .mxd, the shapefiles, raster statistics and the conversations of the time; every element is tagged [C] confirmed / [D] inferred / [to be completed].
Data BD TOPO (IGN): 43,912 buildings, 1,131 vegetated areas, 626 water bodies, 254 + 307 hydrographic segments, tidal flats and the land/sea boundary; ADMIN EXPRESS: municipal boundaries and population; Enedis / open data: electricity consumption for 42 IRIS units, joined and converted into consumption per unit area; CORINE Land Cover 1990 / 2000 / 2006 / 2012: diachronic analysis, artificialisation rising from 74.2% to 78%. Method Project everything to RGF93 / Lambert 93 (EPSG:2154, metres), otherwise areas and distances are meaningless; Union + Feature To Point: each building or green area contributes once, weighted by its own area; Two-pass kernel density (small then large radius): a single kernel produces a bell shape and cannot express both “strong at contact” and “weak at distance”; combining two passes gives a gradient that decays with distance; Mask to the municipal boundary; Normalise, invert the limiting criteria, weighted sum (multi-criteria analysis, MCA): S = 0.50 · B* + 0.33 · (1 - V*) + 0.17 · (1 - E*) Buildings are aggravating, vegetation and water are limiting, so the latter two must be inverted; otherwise more vegetation would increase the computed sensitivity — the classic sign error in multi-criteria analysis.
Results Statistics read directly from the .aux.xml delivered with the rasters:
Raster Cell Max Mean Building heat effect 35.5 m 0.0619 0.00754 Vegetation cooling 33.5 m 0.0190 0.00438 Water cooling 44.4 m 0.0011 0.00015 The maximum building effect is 3.3× vegetation and 55× water. Dunkirk is a territory dominated by buildings, with fragmented vegetation and localised water: 78% of the surface is artificialised, 39% of it industrial and transport land.
The most sensitive areas are the dense city centre, the port-industrial front and large facilities; the least sensitive are the large basins, dunes and tidal flats, and the agricultural fringe to the south. The report’s key point is not “where it is hot” but where compensation is missing: places with strong building effect and weak vegetation accumulate both penalties, and those are the priorities for public action.
Limitations The original report is lost and docs/ is a reconstruction; the weights (0.50 / 0.33 / 0.17) and kernel parameters (search radius, kernel function) were not preserved and are now defensible reconstructions, not original values; the three rasters have different cell sizes (35.5 / 33.5 / 44.4 m), so combining them triggers implicit resampling — a real flaw of the original work, discussed critically in the report; the figures were re-rendered from the rasters, not exported from the original ArcMap layout; there is no field validation, and the index is static: it ignores population exposure and behaviour. Links Report (FR/ZH), technical appendix, ArcMap project and re-rendering script: https://github.com/yicongl1/Dunkerque-Heatwave-Sensitivity
summary: An ArcGIS study that decomposes ‘why cities heat up’ into three continuous fields — building heat, vegetation cooling and water cooling — combines them with two-pass kernel density and multi-criteria weighting, and produces a heatwave sensitivity index for Dunkirk. The building effect is about 3.3× vegetation and 55× water.
title: Dunkirk heatwave sensitivity

contents:
Background vehicleShare is a peer-to-peer car-rental platform: owners publish listings and availability windows, individual or corporate tenants book online, sign a rental contract, inspect the car at pick-up and return, and finally receive an invoice covering rent, excess mileage and missing fuel. Beyond price, the platform also handles ratings, reports, insurance, options and the countries where the car may be driven.
This was the four-person NF18 “Relational and Non-Relational Database Design” course project at UTC, completed in spring 2024. The brief was not a working CRUD demo: it was the whole path from requirements to database — UML class diagram, relational model (MLD), PostgreSQL tables and constraints, a Python command-line application, a normalisation analysis, and finally a NoSQL variant storing semi-structured data in JSON columns.
Data model The model has four parts:
Users: a parent Utilisateur table (login, password, type, active flag) and subtype tables Proprietaire, Locataire, Entreprise; companies also own Conducteur records. Vehicles: Vehicule is keyed by registration number and linked to its owner, insurance contract, availability periods, options and permitted countries. Transaction chain: Annonce → Contrat_location → Etat_des_lieux (one at pick-up, one at return) + Facture + Commentaire. Many-to-many relations: Est_disponible, Peut_circuler and Possede, each with a composite primary key. Implementation highlights Push integrity into the database. Phone format with CHECK (telephone LIKE '__________'), age >= 18, rating 0..5, fuel 0..1; a contract must be either an individual or a company: CHECK ((locataire IS NOT NULL AND entreprise IS NULL) OR (locataire IS NULL AND entreprise IS NOT NULL)). Business rules can be constraints too. A listing with three reports must be inactive, expressed as CHECK (NOT(nombre_signalement >= 3 AND activite)). No application path can bypass it. Parameterised queries with psycopg2. Login, duplicate checks, inserts and deletes mostly use %s placeholders; the application handles menus, permissions and date validation, while the database enforces structure, foreign keys and row-level consistency. The NoSQL variant changes only what it should. Vehicule.contrat_assurance, Contrat_location.commentaire and Contrat_location.facture become JSON columns; the three corresponding tables disappear and queries use ->>, for example WHERE Contrat_assurance->>'type' = 'Tous risques'. Outcome and reflection The repository keeps the five formal submissions (requirements, UML/MLD, SQL, Python application, normalisation) plus the NoSQL extension. Read in order, it shows a database moving from an idea to a queryable structure.
Looking back, the valuable part is not one SQL statement but a few decisions:
which rules must live in the database and which belong in the application; when to model inheritance with subtype tables and when to use one table with a type field; JSON columns remove tables, but they also remove constraints, indexes and easy aggregation. Source, SQL scripts, report and NoSQL variant: https://github.com/yicongl1/Vehicle-Share-Database
summary: Designed the vehicleShare platform from requirements and UML to a PostgreSQL implementation: 18 tables, integrity constraints, a Python/psycopg2 command-line application, and a NoSQL variant storing insurance, invoices and reviews in JSON columns.
title: Vehicle-sharing platform database (UTC-NF18)

contents:
Background A mechanical differential solves a very concrete problem: in a turn, the outer wheel travels a longer arc than the inner wheel. If both wheels are locked to one rigid axle and must turn at the same speed, the tyres scrub against the road — at best extra wear, at worst a loss of control.
Distributed drive offers another answer: give each rear wheel its own motor and adjust their speeds so that each follows its own turning radius. That is an electronic differential.
This was a 2021–2022 “Yunchuang Sino-European” innovation competition project at the Sino-European School of Technology, Shanghai University. Starting from a comparison of drive layouts, the project produced three things: a pygame visualisation of the differential, an Arduino rear-drive model car, and a Keras regression example validating a neural-network workflow.
Design Three layouts were compared:
Centralised drive: one motor plus a mechanical differential — mature, but the speed relationship is fixed by hardware. In-wheel distributed drive: fully independent wheels, the most control freedom, but also the highest cost and unsprung mass. Dual-motor distributed drive: one motor per rear wheel, front-wheel steering retained, differential implemented in software — the practical compromise for a model car. The final design is dual-motor rear drive with front servo steering: the two rear wheels are driven by the two H-bridges of an L298N, an MG995 servo sets the front steering angle, and an IR remote issues forward, backward, left and right commands.
Principle At low speed and neglecting tyre slip, the turn can be described with a simplified Ackermann model:
R = L / tan(δ) v_inner = v · (R - B/2) / R v_outer = v · (R + B/2) / R where L is the wheelbase, B the track width, δ the front steering angle, and R the turning radius at the rear axle. The speed ratio depends only on geometry:
v_outer / v_inner = (R + B/2) / (R - B/2) The model car has a wheelbase of about 0.16 m and a track of about 0.12 m. At a 30° steering angle, R ≈ 0.277 m and the ratio is about 1.55: at 1 m/s the inner wheel runs at about 0.78 m/s and the outer at about 1.22 m/s. The code has no encoders and no closed loop; it translates this relationship into fixed duty cycles — 180 on both sides going straight, 120 inside and 180 outside when turning left, and the reverse when turning right.
Implementation Controller: Arduino Uno, analogWrite PWM into the L298N IN1–IN4 inputs; the Servo library drives the MG995 at 45° / 90° / 135°. Remote: HX1838 IR receiver on D3, using the legacy IRremote 2.x IRrecv / decode_results API; key codes are printed over serial at 9600 baud. Power: two 18650 cells into the L298N 12V / GND terminals, with Arduino and L298N sharing ground; the servo should have its own 5 V supply to avoid brown-outs when the motors start. Visualisation: the pygame animation maps wheel speed to colour depth and shows a direction arrow and steering angle; it evolved from v1.0’s colour mapping to v2.0’s road background and wheels rotating with the steering angle. Documentation: the competition paper, project plan and technical route, electronic-differential research, IR and servo debugging notes, and the build summary are all in docs/. Results and limitations The car drives forward, backward, turns left and right, and stops; the animation makes the inner/outer speed difference visible. It is a good teaching and concept-validation platform, but not a complete electronic-differential controller:
there are no wheel-speed sensors: PWM is open loop, so battery voltage and ground friction change the actual speeds; front steering is open loop, with no angle feedback; there is no current, speed or yaw-rate loop, so slip and load transfer are not handled; the Keras example uses the Boston Housing dataset; it validates the regression workflow only and is not trained on vehicle data. The smallest useful closed-loop upgrade would be: encoders on the rear wheels with a left/right speed PID, a potentiometer or angle sensor on the steering servo, and a target speed ratio computed from the measured steering angle instead of a fixed 120/180 table.
Source, animation, Arduino sketch, paper and notes: https://github.com/yicongl1/EV-Electronic-Differential
summary: Replacing the mechanical differential with two independently driven rear wheels: an Arduino Uno + L298N + two TT motors model car, a pygame animation of the inner/outer wheel speed difference, and the competition paper, technical route and a Keras regression example.
title: Dual-motor distributed drive and electronic differential

contents:
Background Gram–Schmidt orthogonalisation comes in two versions that are equivalent on paper:
Classical (CGS): each vector has all its projections subtracted at once; Modified (MGS): each projection is applied immediately, and the updated vector is used for the next one. In exact arithmetic both produce the same orthonormal basis. In floating point, the order of operations decides whether rounding errors are amplified by later steps. The project asked how large the difference is, when it appears, and why.
Chen Nuo and I completed the project: MATLAB implementations of both algorithms and the experiments, an independent C reproduction, and ill-conditioned and random matrices to quantify the gap.
The two algorithms Classical Gram–Schmidt subtracts every projection in one pass:
u_k = v_k - Σ_{j<k} <v_k, u_j> u_j The modified version splits the projections, updating the vector between them:
v_k ← v_k - <v_k, u_j> u_j, j = 1..k-1 In code the difference is one index: CGS always uses the original column a(:,i) for the dot product, while MGS uses the already updated b(:,i). The whole experiment turns on that line.
Experimental design Run CGS and MGS on the same matrix to obtain Q_CGS and Q_MGS; measure the difference with the Frobenius norm ‖Q_CGS − Q_MGS‖_F; build an ill-conditioned matrix with a very small ε to amplify rounding errors; generate 100 random 100×100 matrices with cond > 10⁶, plot the condition-number/error curve, and repeat the experiment four times. Results Matrix Size cond(A) ‖Q_CGS − Q_MGS‖_F A = [[1,2,3],[2,−1,2],[1,1,2]] 3×3 53.94 5.92×10⁻³¹ (numerically zero) B = [[1,1,1],[ε,0,0],[0,ε,0],[0,0,ε]], ε = 10⁻¹⁰ 4×3 1.73×10¹⁰ 0.2679 The conclusions are direct:
for a small condition number the two algorithms agree numerically; at a very large condition number the columns are nearly linearly dependent, cancellation in the projection becomes severe, the CGS error is amplified from step to step, while the MGS error stays local to each projection; MGS is therefore numerically more stable, which is why numerical libraries use MGS (or Householder QR). C implementation main.c turns the algorithm into an executable: produitscalaire computes a dot product, norme1 normalises, and the main loop orthonormalises column by column. The input is the number of columns, the number of rows, then the matrix row by row; the current implementation requires a square matrix of at most 100×100.
gcc -O2 -Wall -o gs main.c -lm printf "3 3\n1 2 3\n2 -1 2\n1 1 2\n" | ./gs The output matches MATLAB’s Q. The code deliberately transposes on input and output — it stores a[j][i] — so that each column is contiguous in memory and the column-vector loops have a natural access order.
Limitations square matrices only, at most 100×100; no column pivoting and no reorthogonalisation, so linearly dependent columns divide by zero or produce a meaningless basis; the C version implements CGS, not MGS; replacing a[i] with b[i] in the dot product gives MGS, but the repository keeps the classical version used in the report. For real computation, Householder QR is the safer choice, or Gram–Schmidt followed by a reorthogonalisation pass.
MATLAB scripts, C implementation, French report and experiment figures: https://github.com/yicongl1/Linear-Algebra-Gram-Schmidt
summary: Implemented classical Gram–Schmidt (CGS) and the modified version (MGS) in MATLAB and C, compared the two orthonormal bases in Frobenius norm on ill-conditioned matrices and 100 random 100×100 matrices, and explained why formulas that are equivalent on paper separate in floating point.
title: Gram–Schmidt orthogonalisation: a numerical comparison

contents:
Background Data Structures is a core course in the Information Engineering programme at Shanghai University. Its scope runs from lists, stacks and queues to strings, arrays and generalised lists, then trees, heaps, Huffman trees and union-find, and finally graph traversal, minimum spanning trees, shortest paths, topological sorting and critical paths.
This repository collects the course labs, the final assignment and study notes along three lines: course chapters, integrative projects and learning material. Chapters 3–7 contain 36 topic modules plus two integrative projects; the core structures are written with C++ templates.
Repository layout src/ ├── chapter03_linear_list/ # sequential list, singly/doubly linked lists, polynomials, sets ├── chapter04_stack_queue_recursion/ # stacks, queues, expression evaluation, Hanoi, rail shunting ├── chapter05_string_array_generalized_list/ # brute force, KMP, sparse matrices, generalised lists ├── chapter06_tree/ # binary trees, threaded trees, min-heap, Huffman, union-find ├── chapter07_graph/ # DFS/BFS, Prim/Kruskal, Dijkstra/Bellman-Ford/Floyd ├── exercises_cpp_basics/ # first two weeks of C++ exercises └── final_project_leaf_count/ # final assignment: count binary-tree leaves A typical module has three files: Assistance.h for status codes, exceptions and traversal helpers; a structure header such as SeqList.h or BinaryTree.h for the template implementation; and Test*.cpp, a runnable demo entry.
Technical points Templates: sequential lists, linked lists, stacks, queues, binary trees and graphs all use template <class ElemType>, so one implementation can hold int, double, string or a user type. Status codes instead of exceptions: insert, delete and get return SUCCESS, RANGE_ERROR, OVER_FLOW or NOT_PRESENT, and the caller must handle failure explicitly. It is the course style, and it makes edge cases visible. A complete algorithm spectrum: from O(1) sequential access to O(n+m) KMP, then Prim / Kruskal / Dijkstra / Bellman-Ford / Floyd, topological sorting and critical paths. Final assignment: count leaves in a binary linked tree. A null child returns 0, a node with no children returns 1, otherwise recurse into both subtrees; O(n) time and O(h) space. Code verification After reorganising, I ran g++ -fsyntax-only over all 38 demo entry points: 35 / 38 pass. The three failures come from the original course code and were left untouched:
chapter03_linear_list/seq_list/SeqList.h: getElem in the copy constructor should be GetElem; chapter03_linear_list/set_intersection/SeqList.h: the same typo in an independent copy; exercises_cpp_basics/Project1/main.cpp: the original demo entry has a pointer/reference parameter mismatch and is an unfinished draft. Keeping them is deliberate: the repository is a course record first and a portfolio second. Cleaning up the original code would remove its value as study material; the README, however, must say what runs and what does not.
What I took away The real training was not memorising algorithms, but three habits:
separate the logical structure (linear, tree, graph) from the physical one (sequential, linked); compare implementations by complexity, not by “it feels fast”; make every module compile, run and be verified on its own. Course notes, weekly lab logs, selected lecture handouts and run screenshots are in docs/.
Source and documentation: https://gitee.com/yicongl1/data-structures-cpp
summary: Organised seven chapters of course work into 36 topic modules and two integrative projects: C++ templates for lists, stacks, queues, trees and graphs, covering KMP, Huffman, union-find, minimum spanning trees, shortest paths, topological sort and critical paths.
title: Data structures: C++ templates and course labs
